title: Where Fahrenheit's zero came from
hook: Zero degrees Fahrenheit was a bucket of ice, water and salt.
peek: Daniel Fahrenheit did not pick his zero at random. He set it at the temperature of a freezing salty slush he could make on demand, which is why water freezes at the strange-looking figure of 32.
lede: In the early 1700s Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, an instrument maker from Danzig working in Amsterdam, needed fixed points that anyone could reproduce. In a 1724 paper he described his zero: a mix of ice, water and sal ammoniac, a type of salt. Salt lowers the freezing point, so the slush settles at a temperature well below that of plain ice water.

bullets.text: Fahrenheit used three markers. Zero was the salty ice mix, 32 was ice in plain water, and 96 was the warmth of a healthy person, measured in the mouth or under the arm.

Fahrenheit visited the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer in Copenhagen in 1708. Rømer already used a scale with fixed points for freezing water and body heat, and Fahrenheit adapted it, multiplying the numbers to give finer degrees.
A popular story says zero was the coldest day of the hard winter of 1708 to 1709 in Danzig. It makes a neat tale, but Fahrenheit's own paper describes the salt mixture instead.
The scale was later recalibrated so that water boils at exactly 212 degrees, 180 above freezing. That small shift moved normal body temperature from 96 to about 98.6.
